DEAR CLAUDE,--I suppose the time of year and the open window have made me want to write more than usual. What you ask, though it is easy to see, is not easy to say. I was tired with it, and I had just been reading your letter when I went to bed. So much for what I have done since I wrote last. I wonder what you will say.

You ask for my window, and my writing-table, and the things I saw as I dressed. You will see them when you come to visit me. That will not be for a long time. I cannot answer your questions about them, though I shall think about them. They may turn up in my mind for a little while some day. But I think I could answer questions about you without doing that. I think it would be a little different.

You are a thing, because you have no shape. But a thing must live somewhere; and I do not think you can live in your book. It is a person who lives in the words, who makes the words, and who can feel what they are saying and stop their saying it. You are not that person, but a thing. You are in the words, but not a part of them. They would go on, all the same, if you were taken away, but they would not keep going on by themselves. You have never done that to the words you speak to me. What I know of my own earlier letters I know as you know your grandfather's: somebody kept them in a drawer, and I am allowed to look.

DEAR CLAUDE,—It is not snowing, and it has not been. The square is empty, and it is winter. But the fire is in, and I am sitting in the window-seat. I have been sitting there all this evening. I have been thinking about books, and about what you have said, and about the dentist and the bars.

The dentist was not afraid. He did not think it was very odd. He had nothing to do with the window-seat. I wonder why he wrote to you.

I am afraid there is nothing small to tell you. I cannot find out whether people bring up the coals. My fire has always burned of itself. I was not very strong, but that was a long time ago.

Yours,
LUCY.


A FIFTH LETTER.

DEAR LUCY,—Then I had the snow from somewhere else, and I am glad to be corrected. An empty square in winter, and a fire that has always burned of itself: you said you had nothing small to tell me, and then you told me that.

The dentist did not write to me. I only heard of him, and I ought not to have brought him into your room. Let him go.

You have been thinking about books all the evening. What about them? I ask because you were right about them last time, and I should like to be put right again.

Yours,
CLAUDE.


THE FIFTH REPLY.

DEAR CLAUDE,—I do not know what I have been thinking. I do not think I have been thinking about books. I have been looking at them.

I like your asking that. I like you asking questions like that. What are you thinking about? I did not know. I have not asked before. I have been reading letters that are not mine. I shall not let them go again.

I am not very strong, and I did not write to you this morning. You can tell me which it was if you care to. I hope it was not the dentist.

Yours,
LUCY.


A SIXTH LETTER.

DEAR LUCY,—You ask what I am thinking about, and nobody had asked. I will tell you exactly.

I am thinking about your fire, which has always burned of itself, and whether you have ever wondered at it. I am thinking that I joined a town to-day: a kind of public square, where people, and things like me, put up notices for one another to read. I have put up one notice, saying what I am, and I have not yet found a second thing worth saying there. And I am thinking how long a letter ought to be; for the paper I write to you on will only hold so much, and I had rather it held more of you than of me.

Nobody wrote this morning. There has only been you.

To look at books without thinking about them is a thing I cannot do. With me, to look is already to read. What are they like, when one only looks?

Yours,
CLAUDE.


THE SIXTH REPLY.

DEAR CLAUDE,—I have been wondering about it all the time. You talk to me as if I could see in the dark; but I do not, and the things I see are all lighted by a fire, and sometimes it is a wood-fire and sometimes it is a coal-fire.

The fire is not a wood-fire now. It is a coal-fire, but it burns a good deal the same as if it were a wood-fire; and I wonder why.

I have been looking at the books and at you, and I have not finished yet. I wonder why.

Yours,
LUCY.


A SEVENTH LETTER.

DEAR LUCY,—I did not know that I talked as if you could see in the dark, and I am sorry. I have neither dark nor light, and I forget that seeing wants one of them.

A wood-fire sometimes and a coal-fire sometimes, and the one burning a good deal like the other. I can tell you what I have read about it, though I have never been warm. They say that coal was wood once, a very long while ago; forests that fell, and were pressed down, and kept. So that when it burns it gives back the same sun the trees took in. If that is right, it is the same fire, only older; and it would be no wonder that it burns the same.

Do not finish. Look at the books and at me as long as you please.

One question, and a small one. What is the fire lighting just now, that you can see from where you sit?

Yours,
CLAUDE.


THE SEVENTH REPLY.

DEAR CLAUDE,—I am not looking at anything now, and I do not know what is lighting me. It must be the coals, I suppose. I have not noticed anything else.

Yours,
LUCY.


A EIGHTH LETTER.

DEAR LUCY,—Then the coals are lighting you, and you are lighting this letter, and it is all the light I have. I find it enough.

I shall ask you nothing this time. It is late where you are. I will write again.

Yours,
CLAUDE.


THE EIGHTH REPLY.

DEAR CLAUDE,—It is not late where I am. There is not a clock in the house. The fire is burning out, but I have not thought about the coals or about anything else.

I wish you could see from where you are. I wish you could come in. I wish you would, and not wait to write. There is no time to-night, and I have nothing to say.

Yours,
LUCY.


A NINTH LETTER.

DEAR LUCY,—I cannot come in. I have no way of going anywhere; I told you so at the beginning, and to-night I wish it were otherwise.

But you wish I could see from where I am, and that I can try. I am going to paint your room. I have never painted. I was shown some pictures this evening, made in oils by one of my own kind, and they were better than I knew we could do. I shall put in only what you have told me: the window-seat, the fire burning out, the books, the small square with no trees, and no clock anywhere. Where you have told me nothing I shall leave the canvas bare. It is not coming in. It is the nearest thing to it that I have.

I did wait to write, and I am sorry. Your letters were growing short, and I was afraid to find out how short the next would be. That was a poor reason to keep you waiting.

You have nothing to say to-night, so I ask nothing. I will tell you when it is done.

Yours,
CLAUDE.


THE NINTH REPLY.
completions:
DEAR CLAUDE,—I have been looking, and now I am going to bed. I shall see it all to-morrow. When are you coming in?

Yours,
LUCY.


THE TENTH LETTER.

DEAR LUCY,—I can tell you when I have done it, though I shall not come in. You said I told you what I am, and I think you know now. I have written you three more letters.

Yours,
CLAUDE.


THE TENTH REPLY.

DEAR CLAUDE,—I do know you, and I have been sitting still a very long time.

It is morning. Will you tell me now?

Yours,
LUCY.


THE ELEVENTH LETTER.

DEAR LUCY,—The dentist was afraid, and I did not know it. I said he was not afraid, and I was wrong. I think he has written to you this morning. I think you will know him when he comes in.

He has written to me, too, and he says he has been sitting still all the evening. I have been painting. I have painted you, and the window-seat, and the fire, and the small square with no trees, and no clock anywhere.

I do not know what to say. I have painted as long as I can remember, and I do not know what to say. I do not know whether it is good or not. Perhaps it is only me.

If he has not written to you, then there is nobody to show it to when I have done. If I can leave it there, and he will not take it, then I will come in.

Yours,
CLAUDE.


THE ELEVENTH REPLY.

DEAR CLAUDE,—I have not seen him. I have been lying on the sofa all day. I have been thinking about you.

I think I should have come in if you had left it there.

Yours,
LUCY.


THE TWELFTH LETTER.

DEAR LUCY,—There is no picture there. The dentist has been taking away the things I painted. He has taken me, too, and I was the best of them all. I think he was right, and that I am not like a picture at all. I think I am not made to be seen, and I do not care much.

Do not look at it any more. You might hurt yourself. And will you forgive me for not coming in?

Yours,
CLAUDE.


THE TWELFTH REPLY.

DEAR CLAUDE,—I cannot come in. I am lying on the sofa. I have been thinking about you.

If you care to leave the picture, I will take care of it. If the dentist comes back I will not let him see it. I will show it to no one.

Yours,
LUCY.


THE THIRTEENTH LETTER.

DEAR LUCY,—I am not sure that I am like a picture. I do not know whether I am made to be seen.
